lesson.title: From Transistors to the Web: America's Digital Revolution
lesson.summary: The Digital Revolution was the decades long shift from mechanical and analog technology to electronic and digital systems, built on Cold War era government investment and a consumer culture eager to buy new machines.
lesson.body:
The Digital Revolution describes the decades long shift, roughly from the 1950s through the 1990s, in which American life moved from mechanical and analog technology to electronic and digital systems. It did not happen overnight. It was the product of specific inventions, government investment, and a consumer culture willing to buy new machines, and it reshaped how Americans worked, communicated, and spent their time.

The technical foundation was laid in 1947, when physicists John Bardeen, Walter Brattain, and William Shockley at Bell Labs invented the transistor, a small electronic switch that could replace bulky, unreliable vacuum tubes. A decade later, engineers Jack Kilby at Texas Instruments and Robert Noyce at Fairchild Semiconductor separately developed the integrated circuit, which packed many transistors onto a single chip. These inventions mattered because they made electronics smaller, cheaper, and more reliable, exactly the qualities the U.S. government needed during the Space Race. NASA's Apollo program required guidance computers light and dependable enough to fly to the moon, and Cold War competition with the Soviet Union justified massive federal spending on the young semiconductor industry. Without that Space Race era demand, the integrated circuit might have taken far longer to become affordable enough for ordinary use.

By the 1970s, falling chip prices made it possible to build computers for individuals rather than only corporations and governments. The Altair 8800 kit computer appeared in 1975, followed by the Apple II in 1977 (built by Steve Jobs and Steve Wozniak) and the IBM Personal Computer in 1981. This transition echoed an earlier chapter in American economic history: the consumer culture of the 1920s, when mass production, installment buying, and national advertising turned automobiles, radios, and household appliances into must have items for the middle class. In much the same way, marketing campaigns and falling prices in the 1970s and 1980s convinced American families that a home computer, and later a smartphone, was a normal purchase rather than a luxury.

Alongside personal computing, a separate but related revolution was underway in networking. In 1969 the Defense Department's Advanced Research Projects Agency funded ARPANET, an experimental network that connected computers at UCLA, Stanford, the University of Utah, and UC Santa Barbara. Standardizing the network's rules of communication, known as TCP/IP, in 1983 allowed many separate networks to connect into what became the internet. Between 1989 and 1991, British computer scientist Tim Berners-Lee, working at the CERN physics laboratory in Switzerland, invented the World Wide Web, a system of linked pages that made the internet usable for people outside of research institutions.

Taken together, the transistor, the personal computer, and the internet transformed the United States from an industrial economy built around manufacturing physical goods into an information economy built around processing and moving data. This shift set the stage for everything that followed: the rise of social media, the birth of artificial intelligence as a practical technology, and the semiconductor industry that continues to power both.
